title: South-east Australia lost a near-constant fraction of runoff in every month after 1997; in a monthly model, warming accounted for most of the eastern US offset after 2009 (CAMELS, 1948-2025)
abstract: Question: after 1997, runoff in south-east Australia (SE-AU) and the eastern US (East-US) fell about 40 mm/yr below the 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relation. In which months does the water go missing, and which cause has that seasonal fingerprint? Approach: monthly flow and climate for 277 CAMELS-AUS (AGCD and SILO rain, to 2021) and 536 CAMELS-US catchments (USGS flow, nClimGrid, to 2025-09). Two monthly models fitted on 1951-1996 only: a per-month regression and GR2M with a snow store and Oudin PET. In each calibrated GR2M we simulated eight mechanisms sized to each catchment's deficit and compared predicted and observed month profiles (cluster bootstrap; plan written first). Results: in 179 SE-AU catchments the 2010-2021 deficit was -47 mm/yr (95% CI -62 to -34), 15% of expected flow, and 6-25% in every calendar month; the warm season carried 37% (23-49%). More evapotranspiration (ET) in the growing season only was rejected in both periods (share difference -0.12, CI -0.22 to -0.03); a larger store to fill fitted poorly; cool-season-only ET was rejected after 2009. Proportional, rain-input, year-round ET and groundwater-loss mechanisms agreed and cannot be separated. Warming explained about 7 of 54 mm/yr; at most 20 mm/yr with a post hoc temperature correction. In 258 East-US catchments GR2M left only -10 mm/yr after 2009 (-19 to 0) against -45 for the regression; post hoc, with PET held at its 1951-1996 cycle the deficit was -32, so warming (+1.2 C, +6.6% Oudin PET) accounts for about two thirds in this model. But catchments that warmed more did not lose more (Spearman +0.18), and a 1997-2009 deficit of -16 mm/yr (-24 to -9) in February-March remains. Limitations: two-parameter model with a fixed snow store; similar fingerprints for four mechanisms; temperature-only PET; SE-AU drift before 1997 (placebo -25 mm/yr); post hoc temperature tests.
